Credit Growth in Banking Industry 
*242. SHRI JIBON ROY: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Indian banking industry have shown slow down 
in terms of credit growth during 2000-2001; and 
(b) if so, the reason thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE-PATIL): (a) No, Sir. Credit growth of scheduled 
commercial banks during 2000-2001 (upto Feb. 9, 2001) was Rs. 65,151 crore 
(14.9 per cent) as compared to Rs. 50,886 crore (13.8 per cent) in the 
corresponding period of the previous year. 
(b) Does not arise. 
SHRI JIBON ROY: Sir, if you read the Reserve Bank of India bulletin 
carefully, you will find that growth rate of the bank deposits is coming down with 
every passing year. At the same time, it is also a fact that there is reduction in the 
bank rate. The credit-deposit ratio has also been coming down with every 
passing year. It was 60 per cent in 1990-91. Now, it is around 50 per cent. The 
money is going to safe destinations, to bank securities. The bank security rate 
is increasing year after year. Is it not tr ue that our economic gjpwth is thus 
discouraged? I want to know the perception of the Finance Ministry in this 
regard. What do they think about it? Does it not signify that there is something 
wrong in the economic system? I would like to know from the hon. Minister 
whether the whole thing will be reviewed at his level and corrective measures 
taken. 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March 2001] 
SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL: Sir,  the credit-deposit ratio of the 
banks in some States has improved, but in some States, it has gone down. So 
far as the banks are concerned, there is an overall improvement. Sometimes, it 
is more than 100 per cent. If the hon. Member wants, I can read out from this 
chart. It is only in the cas e of one or two banks, particularly, those that are 
private banks, the ratio is 9 per cent. Bu t in the case most of the States, it is 
not so. I think the hon. Member want s to know about Bengal. The credit-
deposit ratio in Bengal was 43.2 per cent in March 1989. It is 45.2 per cent in 
2001. So, he will find that there too, th ere has been an increase in the credit-
deposit ratio. As far as the interest ra te is concerned, everybody is fully 
aware that prior to the Budget and after the Budget, it is the RBI which is the 
regulating authority. It regulates the interest rate as per the market 
conditions. 
SHRI JIBON ROY: Sir, if the hon. Minister is satisfied with the 
developments, I have nothing to say, but the fact is that the bank is no more 
a rich management system. All our moneys are being deposited in 
Government securities. Even accordin g to the RBI bulle tin, in the third 
quarter itself, the credit, in absolute terms, was less than the previous year. If 
the Government is satisfied, it is very good. Now, I come to my second 
supplementary. 
Sir, if you take the April to October figures for the year 2000-01, you will 
find that in all the priority sectors, the credit has gone down. It has gone down 
even in the agricultural sector, if you keep aside the agro-based industries. 
Kindly see; even Pepsi and Nestle, according to your new circular are in 
agriculture. It you take them away from this, you will find that the credit has 
come down in the agricultural sector also. In the small-scale industries, it is a 
negative growth. Even in large and medium industries, the credit is less than 
the rate of growth of deposits. Therefore, here also, I would like to know 
whether the facts that I am submitting are correct or not? If so, what steps the 
Government has taken to improve the credit ratio in the agricultural sector 
and in the small-scale industries sector? So far as the small-scale industries 
are concerned, they are perishing. They are facing a famine like situation. 
Thousands of workers are losing jobs. Therefore, may I know what steps the 
Gowemment has taken to ameliorate the position?

SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would like to know from 
the hon. Minister whether some banks and the UTI have advanced monies to 
the Stock Exchange brokers, flouting all the norms of the RBI. Now, that is 
one of the reasons for the crisis in the Stock Exchanges. What is the reaction 
of the Government? 
SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE-PATIL: This question does not arise out of 
the main question. 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, there is a question which is coming up separately. I am sure, it 
will be discussed in detail when we take up the Calling Attention Motion. But, 
in response to the question that the hon. Member has asked, I would like to

the norms. The norm is 5 per cent. Of the total advances, they are below 2 
per cent. I have been assured by the Reserve Bank of India that there has 
been no violation of the prudential norms of the RBI in this regard.

Inclusion of Majuli Island as living cultural heritage in UNESCO Map 
*243. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of TOURISM 
AND CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) the list of proposals of Government to include non-archaeological 
living cultural heritage sites of the country in the world heritage map of 
UNESCO and the response received so far; 
(b)' whether the Ministry will also consider to propose inclusion of the 500 
year old living cultural heritage of Majuli Island; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI ANANTH 
KUMAR): (a) to (d) There is no category of non-archaeological living 
cultural heritage site in the UNESCO's World Heritage Convention. However, 
the Ministry of Environment and Forests have requested UNESCO for 
preparatory assistance for nominating Majuli Island as a natural World 
Heritage Site. 
DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Sir, the reply of the hon. Minister gives an 
impression that the Ministry has not gone into the details of the subject. Sir, 
the UNESCO considered three criteria while declaring the world heritage 
sites. The first one is natural sites;  the second one is cultural sites, i.e., 
monuments and archaeological sites; and, the third one is sites having living 
cultural traditions in a natural environment. So far, the Government of India 
considered only monuments for being declared as world heritage sites. Sir, the 
Majuli Island of Assam happens to be the biggest fresh water river island in 
the world and fulfils criteria v and vi of the Charter of the UNESCO, which 
deals with declaring the world heritage sites. Firstly, criterion v says, I quote, 
"Be an outstanding example of a traditional human settlement or land use 
which is representative of a culture (or cultures), especi ally when it has 
become vulnerable, under the impact of irreversible change." Secondly, 
criterion vi says, I quote, "Be directly or tangibly associated with events or 
living traditions, with ideas, or with beliefs, with artistic and literary works of 
outstanding universal significance." Sir, the Majuli Island of Assam has 
maintained a living Vaishnavite cultural tradition founded by Shriman 
Shankara Deva and has been maintained for more than 500 years in its trust 
form, in a natural environment. It fulfils both the criteria, as have been 
referred. I would like to know from the hon. Minister whether he will direct 
the concerned Ministry to re-examine the issue and take necessary action for 
nominating the Majuli Island as a world living cultural heritage site. 
SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: Sir, for nomination, the UNESCO has 
classified the sites of importance into three categories—natural sites, cultural 
sites and mixed sites. I appreciate the intent of the hon. Member. I also feel 
that the Majuli Island in Jorhat, falls both under the natural as well as the 
cultural category. It is a mixed site because

living cultural heritage site. Such a classification is not there in the UNESCO.

Import Duty of Indian Tea 
*248. SHRI K.M. SAIFULLAH: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Egypt has imposed thirty per cent import duty on Indian tea 
against three per cent levied for Kenyan tea; and 
(b) if so, the action proposed to be taken up in the matter with Egypt to 
boost India's export which has come down from 6.65 in 1998 to  1.16 
million kgs in 1999? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE  
AND  INDUSTRY  (SHRI  OMAR ABDULLAH): 
(a) The general rate of import duty on import of bulk and packet teas into 
Egypt including from India is 30%. Si nce Egypt is a me mber of COMESA, 
it extends concession on import duty to other member countries including 
Kenya. The rate of concession exte nded to Kenya on tea is 90% thereby 
bringing the effective rate of import duty on Kenyan tea into Egypt to 3%. 
(b) Government/Tea Board had requested the Egyptian authorities to 
extend similar concessions as being given to COMESA member countries to 
India as well. However, this was not agreed to by Egypt. Alternatively, it has 
been suggested by the Egyptian authorities to identify commodities for 
which import duty could be reduced by both the countries. Notwithstanding 
the import duty issue with Egypt. Tea Board has initiated a number of steps 
to promote export of tea to Egypt and it is expected that as a result of these 
efforts, exports to this country will go up both in volume and value in the 
coming years. 
SHRI K.M. SAIFULLAH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I had put a question with 
regard to the import concession extended to Kenya vis-a-vis India. The 
Minister in his written reply has said, "Since Egypt is a member of the 
COMESA, it extends concession on import duty to other member countries 
including Kenya." Since there is not much time during Question Hour. I will 
put a straightforward question. Why can't the Minister mediate or arbitrate 
with the Egyptian authorities to get import duty concession 
28 

[13 March 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
to India, as has been extended to Kenya? The Minister should speed up the 
process of mediation. 
SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, there is no such 
provision of mediation in this issue. It is a bilateral issue between India and 
Egypt. Egypt is a member of the COMESA Trade Group in Africa, on 
account of which, Kenya gets duty preferential access to the Egyptian 
market. At the same time, we are now exploring the possibility of a 
preferential trade agreement with Egypt. As and wh en such trade agreement 
comes into place, tea, of course, will feature in that. We hope to get duty 
preference access to the Egyptian market. 
SHRI K.M. SAIFULLAH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, my second supplementary 
arises out of the written reply given by  the Minister. "The Government/Tea 
Board had requested the Egyptian authorities to extend similar concessions 
as being given to COMESA member co untries to India as well." But they 
have refused it. Today, wc arc going for an arbitration. To that effect. I want 
a clarification. 
SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH: Mr. Chairman. Sir, -arbitration-means, we 
arc discussing it bilaterally. As I have mentioned, wc have already initiated 
discussions with the Egyptian Government for a possible preferential trade 
agreement. As and when that preferential trade agreement comes about, wc 
will ensure that our tea gets preferential access to the Egyptian market.

Displacement of Families due to Sardar Sarovar Project 
*252. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA : Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that nearly 85,000 families will be 
displaced while completing the Sardar Sarovar Project; 
(b) if so, whether Government are taking proper initiative to save those 
families from obvious disaster; and 
38 

[13 March 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) if so, what are the details of the projects being undertaken for the 
welfare of the displaced families? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESO URCES (SHRI ARJUN CHAR AN 
SETHI): (a) to (c) The Sardar Sarovar Project (SSP) on its completion would 
displace about 40835 families due to s ubmergence and back water effect at 
full height of the dam with FRL 138.68 m. (455 ft.). This includes 33014 
Project Affected Families (PAFs) of Madhya Pradesh, 3221 PAFs of 
Maharashtra and 4600 PAFs of Gujarat. 
Narmada Water Dispute Tribunal (NWDT) in its final orders had given 
detailed directions with regard to ac quisition of land and properties and the 
compensation to be provided to the Project Affected Families (PAFs) for 
their Resettlement and Rehabilitation (R&R). With a view to improve the 
economic conditions of the project affected families after resettlement, the 
party States of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat, have further 
liberalized the package for resettlement and rehabilitation provided by the 
NWDT. The revised package of Gujarat, which is one of the best R&R 
package in the country so far, provides land equivalent to that acquired subject 
to a minimum of 2 ha. for each family. All landless agricultural la bourers, 
encroachers of government land etc. are also allotted 2 ha. of agricultural 
land. Every major son is treated as a separate family for the R&R package. 
Each family is provided a residential plot of 500 Sq. metres free of cost along 
with a core house costing Rs. 45,000/-. In add ition, resettlement grants 
comprising subsistence allowance, grant for ploughing, grant ior purchase of 
productive assets, transportation of building materials and household goods & 
other insurance are provided to each family. 
Civil and other amenities such as appr oach road, internal roads, primary 
school building, health centre, panchayat ghar, seeds store, children's park, 
village pond, drinking water wells, platform for community meetings, street 
light electrification, religious place, crematorium ground etc. are provided at 
resettled site. 
All the three participating State Governments have also established 
independent Grievance Redressel Authorities headed by a Retired 
39

Justice of Supreme Court/High Court to deal with the grievance of the 
displaced persons.

Organisations as it was adverse to Indian farmers and farm workers; 
(b) if so, whether it is obligatory for India to import specified quantity of 
foodgrains even if India has surplus of these grains; and 
(c) what steps are being taken by Government to rectify the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) There have been representations 
from a few organisations from different parts of the country for disassociation 
of India from the WTO mainly on the grounds that WTO agreements have severely 
constrained domestic policy options and have mainly benefited the developed 
countries and the interests of the domestic producers in developing countries have 
been compromised. 
(b) and (c) It is not obligatory for India to import any specified 
76 

[13 March 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
quanitity of foodgrains irrespective of an y situation of surplus or shortage in 
the country, as India has not undertaken any commitment under WTO 
Agreement on Agriculture to provide any minimum market access. It has also 
been specifically indicated in India' s schedule of commitments filed in 
WTO, that even in the event of removal of Quantitative Restrictions, (QRs), 
India would not be required to establish any minimum market access 
opportunities till the end of the implementation period, which is up to the 
end of year 2004. Further, India has also proposed to the WTO in the 
ongoing negotiations that developing countries should be exempted from any 
obligation to provide any minimum market access.

a bank subject to its satisfying the prescribed criteria. 
(iv) The bank shall maintain a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 10 
percent. 
(v) These banks shall also observe th e prescribed priority sector lending 
target.

urban areas. 
(e) and (d) RBI has reported that a comparison of the growth of 
the new private sector banks vis-a-vis the public sector banks reveals 
that there has been an impact on the market share of the public 
sector banks. While the assets of both the public sector banks and the 
new private sector banks have be^en increasing, the share of public 
sector banks in the total assets of the scheduled commercial banks

Settlement of cases of NPAs 
1851. SHRI KHAN GHUFRAN ZAHI DI: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to refer to answer to Unstarred Question 52 given in 
the Rajya Sabha on the 20th February, 2001 and state: 
(a) whether RBI has issued any instructions to the banks for waving off 
huge interest dues on NPAs; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the guidelines issued for settlement of 
such cases; and 
(c) the total amount recovered so far under this scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI.BALASAHEB VIKHE-PATIL): (a) and (b) Reserve Bank of India 
(RBI) have issued guidelines in July, 2000 to all public sector banks for 
recovery of dues relating to Non-Performing Assets (NPAs), through a 
simplified, non-discretionary and non-dicriminatory mechanism. These 
guidelines cover:— 
(i) All NPAs in all sectors irrespective of the nature of business which 
have been become doubtful' or Moss' as on 31st March. 1997 as well 
as "sub-standard" as on 31.3.1997 which have subsequently become 
'doubtful' or 'loss' category, with outstanding balance of Rs. 5 crore 
and below on the cut-off date. 
(ii) Cases pending before Courts/DRTs/BIFR. 
As per the guidelines, the settlement formula and amount will be as 
under:— 
• NPAs classified as Doubtful or Loss as on 31st March, 1997— the 
minimum amount that should be recovered is 100% of the total 
outstanding balance in the account as on the date of transfer to the 
protested bills account or the amount as on the date on which the 
account was categorised as doubtful  NPA whichever happened earlier, 
as the case may be. 
• NPAs classified as Sub-standard as on 31st March, 1997 which 
became doubtful or loss subsequently—the minimum amount that 
should  be  recovered  is   100%  of outstanding balance  in  the 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March 2001] 
account as on the date of transfer to the protested bills account or the 
amount as on the date on which the account was categorised as doubtful 
NPA, whichever happened earlier, as the case may be, plus interest at 
existing Prime Lending Rate from 1st April, 1997, till the date of final 
payment. 
The amount of settlement arrived at in both the above cases, should 
preferably be paid in one lump sum. In deserving cases, at least 25% of the 
amount of settlement should be paid upfront and the balance amount of 75% should 
be recovered within a period of one year togetherwith interest at the existing 
Prime Lending Rate from the date of settlement upto the date of final 
payment. 
As regards NPAs of Rs. 5 crore and above, these guidelines provide for 
personal supervision of such cases by the Chairman & Managing Directors. 
The guidelines will remain operative upto 31.3.2001. 
(c) According to the information available with RBI, as on 31st December, 
2000, the Public Sector Banks recovered a sum of Rs. 793 crores out of the 
NPAs.

Lower economic growth 
1867. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: WiU the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
appearing in the News Time dated 3rd February, 2001 under the caption "WB 
predicts tough times for economy"; 
(b) if so, what is Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to boost the foreign capital flow which as 
per the World Bank report has retained a low in recent 
year? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE-PATIL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) As per India's balance of payments account, India attracted a net capital 
inflow of US $ 8 billion on an average during the five-year period 1995-96 to 
1999-2000 and US $ 2.5 billion during the first half of the current year 2000-
2001. Subsequently, the issues of India Millennium Deposits by the State 
Bank of India helped to raise foreign currency assets amounting to US $ 5.51 
billion. Total foreign exchange reserves (including gold and SDRs) at the end of 
February, 2001 stood at US $ 41.61 billi on, providing cover for 8 months of 
projected imports in 2000-01. Such inflows of foreign capital and build up of 
foreign exchange reserve are considered to be reasonable in the backdrop of the 
current global economic and financial situation which deteriorated remarkably 
in the recent past following the crises in Asia and Russia. 
(c) Steps taken by the Government and the RBI to boost inflow of foreign 
capital include liberalisation of policies relating to non-debt creating financial 
flows such as direct foreign investment and protfollo investment and adopting a 
gradual but cautious approach towards full capital account convertibility.

(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE-PATIL): (a) to (d) With a view to strengthening the 
flow of credit to small and marginal farmers, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has 
extended certain relaxations in regard to margin money requirements, security 
norms, etc. to such borrowers under the priority sector. Some of these relaxations 
are : 
(i) Banks should not insist on margin money for crop loans/ terms loans 
granted to farmers utpo Rs. 10,000/-; 
(ii) banks should not insist upon collateral seciirity/third party guarantee for 
crop loans upto Rs. 10,000*- Hypothecation of crops can be taken as 
security; 
(Ui) As regards loans above Rs. 10,000'- banks have discretion in matters 
relating to margin/security; 
(iv) Payment of interest should be insisted upon only at the time of 
repayment of loan/instalments fixed; 
(v) Banks should not compound interest on current dues in respect of 
long duration crop loans and instalments not falling due in respect 
of term loans; 
(vi) Total interest debited to the account of small and marginal farmers should 
not exceed the principle amount in respect of short-term advances.

Rebate in Income Tax for disabled persons 
1872. SHRI BRATIN SENGUPTA: 
SHRI LALITBHAI MEHTA: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in the recen t past the Central Government have 
done away with the disability percentage for grant of Transport Allowance to its 
employees; 
(b) if so, whether Government also propose to do away with the requirement of 
minimum disability of 50 per cent for the purpose of Income Tax rebate; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): <a) No, Sir. The Central Government have 
not done away with the disability percentage for grant of transport allowance to 
its employees; 
(b) and (c) Does not arise in view of (a) above. Under the Income-tax Act, no 
rebate is allowed for disabled persons. However, certain deductions from taxable 
income are allowed to handicapped taxpayers or taxpayers having 
handicapped dependents. 
(d) The criteria for claiming benefit under a provision of the Income-tax Act 
has to be seen in the context of the specific provision. Specification or non-
specification of disability cannot be a uniform criterion for all provisions 
applicable to the disabled taxpayers.

(d) whether Government propose to announce any package for the revival 
of the weak public sector banks; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI^BALASAHEB VIKHE-PATIL). (a) Yes, Sir. Government of India 
has set up on December 22, 2000 a Hi gh Level Group headed by Shri S.P. 
Talwar, Deputy Governor, Reserve Ba nk of India (RBI) to examine the 
Restructuring Plans of three weak banks. 
(b) and (c) The Group has submitted its recommendations to the 
Government on 31st January, 2001. The Group recommended that 
restructuring of weak banks with requisite capital infusion by the Government 
of India is the best alternative for turn around of three weak nationalized 
banks. It recommended re-capitalization assistance of Rs. 2300 crores over 
two years for the three weak banks to achieve/maintain prescribed capital 
adequacy ratio. The proposed comprehensive restructuring plans of the three 
weak banks contain financial as well as non-financial parameters including 
reduction in cost of deposits, acceleration of NPA recovery, reduction in 
overhead costs and operating expenses, rationalization of branch network, 
hiving off of unprofitable subsidiaries, closure of unviable overseas operations, 
growth of non-fund business, better cash management, optimum 
redeployment of staff, technology upgradation, image building and proper 
succession planning etc.

the Government.

Exemption in Excise Duty in Respect of Paper Mills 
1880. SHRI B.P. SINGHAL: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the reasons for withdrawing the duty difference of 8 per cent between 
non-wood based and wood-based paper mills; 
(b) the reasons for imposing 16 per cent excise duty on paper produced out of 
agro residues when the Particle Board manufactured out of the same raw 
material is exempted from excise duty; 
(c) whether Government propose to provide excise duty exemption on such 
paper so that a large number of paper mills could be saved from closure; 
 
(d) if so, by when; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
180 

[13 March 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) The Government has been following 
the policy to introduce a single rate of 16 per cent excise duty (CENVAT) 
and moving away from partial or complete exemptions. As a result of this 
policy, the 8 per cent excise duty appli cable to paper and paperboard made 
from non-conventional raw materials was raised to 16 per cent in the Budget 
for 2000-2001. However, full exemption from excise duty was provided upto 
3500 tonnes of clearances in a financial year by a mill producing sucb paper 
and paperboard. 
(b) Particle board is an entirely different commodity. In terms of use and 
nature of the product it is not comparable with paper or paperboard. Also, 
particle board is a substitute of wood. The exemption from excise duty to 
particle board was provided keeping all relevant aspects in view. 
(c) There is no such proposal under consideration at present. 
(d) and (c) Do not arise in view of answer to (c) above.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM

International Energy Forum meeting of oil producing and consuming 
countries held at Riyadh, Saudi Arabia from November 17—19, 2000, India 
made a suggestion to the effect that oil exporting countries should consider 
giving concessions to the developing c ountries in the form of discounts, 
deffered payments, soft credit etc. The suggestion was well taken and the need 
to give special consideration to de veloping countries wa s appreciated. The 
matter was also taken up in the bilateral meetings also with the oil exporting 
countries, including Saudi Arabia, Iran, Kuwait, UAE, Indonesia, Algeria, 
Nigeria and Qatar. Each of these countries, during the bilateral discussions 
was appreciative of the concerns of India and the developing countries and 
assured that they would ponder upon the suggestion at their own level and 
collectively. Subsequently, on 14th December, 2000, a proposal was sent to the 
OPEC member countries containing the following:— 
(i) Extension of credit period to 90 days by the oil exporting company 
instead of the normal period of 30 days; 
(ii) A price discount of 20% of the incremental price beyond an 
accepted crude price, say $25 per barrel; and 
(iii) Deferred payment facility at LI BOR for a period of three years for 
incremental amounts due to price increases beyond an agreed level, 
say $ 28 per barrel. 
(b) In response to the Indian proposal, Indonesia and Qatar have responded 
that India's proposal may be considered at the next meeting of the 
Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) scheduled to be 
held in Vienna in mid-March, 2001.

National policy for storing of rain water 
† 1928. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
DR. D. MASTHAN: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated any scheme on national level 
for storing the rain water; 
(b) if so, the details of blue print of the above scheme; and 
(c) the estimated amount to be spent to implement the scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) The 
measures for storing the rain water include construction of small medium and 
large storage reservoir and water harvesting through micro watershed 
development programmes. A live storage capacity of 177 Billion Cubic 
Meters (BCM) has been created for storing rain water by construction of 
large dams and medium projects upto 1995. It has also been estimated that 
about 24 BCM of rain water is stored in 3.5 lakh minor irrigation tanks. 
Projects to add and additional capacity of about 75 BCM are under 
construction and for another 132 BCM are under planning. Water Resources 
development measures are planned, executed and financed by the State 
Government in accordance with their own priority from their plan funds. 
Government of India is also promoting rainwater harvesting through 
Watershed Management Programme, artificial recharge of ground water and 
roof-top rainwater harvesting under the- sector reform project of Accelerated 
Rural Water Supply Programme under the Ministry of Rural Development, for 
which technical and financial assistance is provided to the State Governments 
and other implementing agencies. Central Ground Water Board has also 
taken up pilot studies for artificial ground water recharge. 
The Central Ground Water Board under Ministry of Water Resources is 
implementing a Central Sector pilot scheme of artificial recharge to ground 
water through rain water harvesting in different parts of the country at an 
estimated cost of Rs. 25 crore. Under this, schemes worth Rs. 1714.87 lakhs 
have been approved.

CALLING ATTENTION TO MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC 
IMPORTANCE 
The Extreme Volatility in Stock Markets 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Calling Attention to matter of urgent public 
importance.   Dr. Manmohan Singh. 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH (Assam): Sir, I beg to call the 
attention of the Minister of Finance  to the extreme volatility in the 
stock markets In the last few day s which has led to a climate of 
uncertainty and instability for investment and remedial measures 
taken by Government with regard thereto. 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE  (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA): 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, stock markets world wide have been on a 
downtrend, particularly technology st ocks, for the last one year. This 
has also affected Indian markets. For instance, NASDAQ, which 
consists mainly of "new" economy stocks has declined by about 59 
per cent from March, 2000 to March, 2001. The markets in Japan, 
Korea, Taiwan and Germany went down in the last one year by about 
50%, 40%, 55% and 71% respecttvef y. The BSE Sensex decreased 
by 22% in the last one year or so. In line with international technology 
stock Indices the Indian technolog y stocks have also declined by 
about 63%. 
240 

[13 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
While the downwarc movement of the Indian stock market 
and its volatility have not been unusual compared to international 
markets, around the beginning of March, 2001. SEBI received 
information that stock prices we re being manipulated. As such, 
investigations were initiated by SEBI in coordination with NSE, BSfE 
and CSE on 2nd March, 2001 against 20 brokerage entities. 
Subsequently, SEB called a meet ing of stock exchanges in 
Mumbai on 5 ,fl March, 2001 to review the current market situation. 
Thereafter, the following measures were taken by SEBI: 
1. SEBI has imposed a 10% margin on all sales for non-
institutional players effective from 5,h March, 2001. 
2. The threshold limit for applicability of the volatility margin to 
be reduced from the present 80% to 60%. 
3. No exemptions to be allowed in the applicability of volatility 
margin to any class of investors. 
4. All sales transactions effective from 8 m March, 2001 shall be 
backed by delivery unless a sale transaction is preceded by a 
purchase position of at least an equivalent amount in the 
name of the same client In ti e same or any other exchange. 
This will also apply to proprietary trading by members. This 
decision will be reviewed after two settlements. 
The current margining system will be moved to the Value-at-Risk 
(VAR) scrip-wise model from July 1, 2001. 
On 11 th March, 2001, SEBI announced the following 
additional measures to enhance marke: safety:- 
(i) As   a   temporary   measure,   banks   will   be   allowed   to   
provide collateralised funding in Automated Lending and Borrowing 
Mechanism (ALBM) and Borrowing and Lending Securities Scheme 
(BLESS) facilities of the stock exchanges; 
(Ii) The existing trade guarantee funds set up by stock  xchanges  
would henceforth provide counterparty guarantee for all the 
transactions which take place on stock exchanges and meet the 
payment obligations of brokers immediately without waiting to declare 
them as defaulters; 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2001]  
(iii) Henceforth, the securities lending scheme would be 
applicable only to the transac tions under the ALBM/BLESS 
facilities; 
(iv) The additional margin of 10 per cent on the "end of the day" 
net outstanding sale position of all scrips in Modified Carry 
Forward Scheme (MCFS)/A LBM and BLESS introduced 
temporarily by the SEBI on Ma rch 5, 2001 is being increased 
to 25 per cent with effect from March 12, 2001; 
(v) The broker-wise end of the day outstanding position 
(aggregate of all securities) of a member on any stock 
exchange other than the BSE/N SE shall not exceed Rs. 50 
crore; 
(vi) The gross exposure limit for members of the Stock  xchanges 
is being reduced to 10 times of the base capital and the 
additional base capital in the case of NSE and to 15 times for 
the other Stock Exchanges. On I2 ,h March, 2001, SEBI 
announced further measures as below: - 
(a) Anand Rathi, former Presid ent, BSE and his broking concerns 
have been prohibited from undertaking any fresh broking 
business till further orders are passed by SEBI in this regard. 
Anand Rathi has also been restrained from acting as a 
Director Member of the Gove rning Board of BSE till further 
orders. 
(b) In the interest of investors, orderly development of the 
securities market and pr oper management of BSE, six 
members of the Governing Board on BSE have been 
restrained from acting as Directors or office bearers of BSE till 
further orders. 
As far as bank advances against shares and guarantees to 
stock brokers by the banking sy stem is concerned, the RBI has 
intimated that It is less than 2 per cent of the total advances as of 31 s' 
December, 2000. In this regard, according to information available 
with RBI, there has been no violation of its prudential norms. 
While fluctuations are normal in stock markets and should not 
be a matter of undue concern we should be vigilant with regard to any 
systemic risk or movements driven by any form of manipulation. I 
have been assured by SEBI that ther e is no systemic risk to the 
market and there is no danger of a payment crisis. 
SEBI has already started its inve stigations as far as price 
manipulation is concerned and will take necessary follow-up action. In 
addition, I propose to take the following measures to improve 
institutional mechanisms and trading practices in our stock markets: 
242 

[13 March, 2001]        RAJYA SABHA 
(a) Corporatisation of stock exchanges by which ownership, 
management, and trading membership would be 
segregated from each other.  Administrative steps will be 
taken and legislative changes, if required, will be 
proposed accordingly. 
(b) Extension of rolling settlement to 200 category "A" stocks 
in Modified Carry Forward Scheme, Automated Lending 
and Borrowing Mechanism and Borrowing and Lending 
Securities Scheme by July, 2001. 
(c) Government intends to propose legislative changes to 
further strengthen the provisions in the SEBI Act, 1902 to 
ensure investor protection. 
To conclude, I would like to reiterate that the Government 
and SEBI will continue to  make every effort to  ensure that capital 
markets operate In an orderly, transparent, safe and fair manner for 
all investors. I would like to assure  the House that the guilty shall be 
brought to book without fear or favour and no one shall be spared. 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Mr. Chairman Sir, I have heard 
with rapt attention what the hon'bl e Finance Minister has told the 
House. The strong, healthy, transparent capital markets are In the 
national interest. But to ensure that the market functions property and 
to protect the interests of genuine investors, we need credible reforms 
backed by credible systems of supervision and monitoring. In the last 
decade, a good deal of effort has gone into this area. But, what Is 
now happening in the stock-markets is a source of worry to all of us 
because all is not well. The hon. Mini ster has stated that It Is only In 
March this year that the Government  or SEBI knew that crises were 
being manipulated. If this is the stat e of information available to the 
Government or SEBI, this reflects very poorly on what is happening in 
the State of Denmark. 
The second point that the hon. Mi nister has made is that he 
has stated, "I have been assured by  SEBI that there is no systemic 
risk to the market and there is no danger of payment crisis'. I hope 
what the hon. Finance Minister has said is right. But I think he knows 
it and everyone else knows it that the markets certainly do not share 
this perception. The over-activity on the part of the SEBI for the last 
several days had not diminished the nervousness of the market and, 
In fact, this morning the market again tumbled. So, there is a crisis of 
disbelief. We were told last week by SEBI that there was no danger of 
payment crisis,  and come 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2001]  
Monday, the market crashes by 140 points. Last night, probably, in 
anticipation of a parliamentary debate, further measures were 
announced. But the markets were not  impressed. So, I respectfully 
submit to the hon. Finance Minister that there is something deeper, in 
the nature of a malaise, that aff licts our stock-markets and that the 
time has come when this should not be put under the carpet. I 
sincerely believe that a mere routine inquiry by SEBI will not serve the 
purpose of ensuring that our markets are cleaned of unhealthy 
influences, unhealthy practices, excessive, rampant and reckless 
speculation, insider trading, price rigging, etc., that have been noticed 
from time to time, not only after March, but also, at least, for the last 
two years in a row. It saddens me that for the third time in two years 
the President of a leading stock exchange in our country, the Mumbai 
Stock Exchange, has to leave his office in ignominy. I think it was in 
March, 1999. that a former Presi dent of the Mumbai Stock Exchange 
had to step down following his alleged involvement in scandals 
relating to breaking into trading systems after market hours. Now, we 
have seen, in the last week, t he fall of another President. A 
distinguished lady took his place.  Last night, the SEBI has removed 
her also. Along with her, they removed seven Directors also. What is 
it? That itself is an indication that  all is not well with the State of 
Denmark. That SEBI did not know that these broker-driven stock 
exchanges were indulging in activities which are detrimental to the 
interests of the investors, is, at large, a sad reflection on the 
functioning of SEBI and on all those associated with it. 
Sir, all over the world, t he markets do fluctuate and all 
markets are increasingly being integrated into the world market. So, a 
certain amount of fluctuation is i nevitable. The NASDAQ is fluctuating 
and it affects the technology stocks. But I regret to say that in the last 
18 months, and sometimes willy-nilly , SEBI has given the impression 
that it is interested in pushing the prices of these so-called new 
economic stocks in a particular direction. 
I think, in violation of the norms of the SEBI, suddenly for 
initial public offerings these new economic stocks were lowered in 
order to ensure that prices behave in a particular way. In view of an 
this where are we going? i would like to tell the hon. Finance Minister 
that it might have come to their notice only in March, 2001 that the 
prices were being manipulated. The public memory is quite sharp. 
Perhaps, he has forgotten that two years ago, talks of a bull operator 
using bank funds to rig up prices of Sterlite, Videocon,  BPL and 
Himachal Futuristics came to our 
244 

[13 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
notice. SEBI had ordered an inquiry. Sir, to the best of my knowledge, 
that inquiry has still not been complete d. If this is the state of policing 
of our stock exchanges, what conf idence can the country have that 
we have a watch-dog which is equal to the task? I would, therefore, 
like to know from the hon. Finance Minister as to what has happened 
to the 1098 inquiry. So what is going on in the stock exchanges today 
is not a phenomenon which arose on the 2nd March. It has been going 
on for quite some time. Technology stocks were being driven up, were 
being ramped up with the help of a particular bull operator and his 
colleagues for more than a year. What did the SEBI -do? You banned 
the short selling. But what did you do when long purchases were 
taking place to ramp up these favoured ten stocks of a particular bull 
operator? I agree that you should investigate if there is a bear caught. 
But you should also investigate if there is a bull caught. In fact bears

things have gone wrong only after the 2°° of March, 2001? What was 
going on and the manner in which certain bull operators were 
manipulating the stock market was not  consistent with the underlined 
fundamentals of the situation. Mo re recently there has been a talk 
once again of the involvement of bank funds in fanning excessive 
speculation in the stock market. The hon. Finance Minister has told us

before the recent proposed merger of  a private sector bank with the

operator has a sizeable stake in that  bank. Furthermore, that bank is 
lending shares to ramp up the prices further. I would like to know from 
the hon. Finance Minister as to what is the true state of affairs with 
regard to this particular matter. I am told that the Reserve Bank of 
India brought this matter to the notic e of SEBI as earty as in October 
or November and asked the SEBI to  find out if there has been any 
rigging or ramping up of the prices of this particular private sector 
bank before the merger  was completed. What has the SEBI done? 
We know that nothing much has been done. Recently, the Reserve 
Bank was compelled to ask the SEBI  to apprise them, latest by 31 st 
March, as to what its assessment is on the charge of price rigging of 
tNs particular share. The hon. Finan ce Minister has talked of certain 
long-term measures. Sir, I welcomed the decision to bring in the 
rolling settlement system.    
245 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2001]  
asked him: "Who has been blocking the introduction of the rolling 
settlement system?" It is the SEBI which has been blocking this rolling 
settlement system on the plea that It will destroy the feel-good-factor 
in our market, that it will, in t he process, depress prices and volume. I 
respectfully submit to the hon. Minister  that it Is not the function of 
SEBI to sit In judgement on what Is the right volume or what is the 
right price. SEBI should be a ring-mas ter, a monitor, to ensure that

a system where every operator expr esses his wish as to where the 
market should go and" where the market s will go, and, in the process,

poor, the small, investors. We have heard about the Budget. We know 
what it has done to the poor people. Those who invest their monies in 
Provident Funds will loose; those who invest their monies in small

returns these poor savers, widows, pensioners and retired persons

"Forget the old economy. Go and In vest your savings in the new

Sir, I could go on. But I think, there is the limitation of time 
and I end by asking the hon. Finance Minister a few specific things. 
First of all, I would like to ask him:  Did SEBI act on its own or It had to 
be persuaded by the Government to act to restore the so-called feel-
good-factor generated by the Budget? in ot her words, when the SEBI 
intervened after the fall in prices on 2 March, was it at the direction of 
the Government or was it done by SEBI on its own? If it did not act on 
its own, responsibility should be fixed for lack of supervision of the 
market. The second thing that I would like to know from him is: What 
is the scope of Investigation being conducted by SEBI? Will it confine 
itself to the role of the so-called bear cartel or to that of the bull cartel 
also, which has been operating for a long time, particularly, with 
regard to some specific stocks, an d whose operations have been the 
talk of the market not just in March, but, at least, for two years in a 
row? There are well-known ten stocks which have been the subject-
matter of the activities of the bull cartel. I do hope that he will ask the 
SEBI to look into that aspect as we ll, not merely confining to what has 
happened in March. That is important. We must know the truth as to 
what happened in the Mumbai Stock Exchange; what the President's 
role in getting the privileged information was and the leaking of that 
privileged information; all these mu st be unearthed.   I think, the 
activities of the so-

[13 March, 2001]           RAJYA SABHA  
called bull cartel should also be in vestigated by the SEBl thoroughly. 
The third question that I have to put to him is: What happened to the 
1098 SEBl inquiry in which certain br okers were involved in rigging 
the prices of Sterlite, Videocon and Himachal Futuristic? Why has the 
SEBl not completed this inquiry although three ye ars have passed? 
The fourth question is: What has been the role of bank funds in 
favouring excessive speculative tendencies in our capital market? 
Has the Reserve Bank asked the SEBl to probe, in particular, the 
share prices of Global Trust Bank before its proposed merger with the 
Unit Trust of India Bank? If so, w hat has been SEBI's finding in this 
regard? My 5 ,h question: I would like you to answer what has been 
SEBI's own rote in encouraging excessive speculation in the so-called 
new economy stock by liberalising unduly listing-norms to favour 
particular promoters and particular companies. 6 question; Is it true 
that Indian markets are characterise d by excessive speculation vis-a-
vis the most other capital markets of the world? What measures are 
being contemplated to deal with this? You have mentioned the 
introduction of the Rolling Settlement System. I welcome this. But why 
is this Rolling Settlement System, which has been recommended for 
a long time, been held up? I am told that it is held up because SEBl

how it is going to be coordinated with this inquiry that the SEBl has 
ordered. Then, Sir, and I say this with great trepidation, rumours are 
afloat that our stock markets t oday are also, unfortunately, being 
funded by underworld money. I would like you to tell us if you had any 
information at your disposal. I hope I am wrong. But these are some 
of the issues that we ex pect the hon. Finance Minister to clarify; and, 
in my view, this debate will serve a purpose, but the matter is far too 
serious. We need an inquiry that will truly inspire confidence. But so 
far as the nature of that inquiry is concerned, I think we can discuss 
that at a later stage.

story of the bulfs. Imagine, Sir.  in the bear stock market what 
happens? A person sells the share an d if the stock is falling, then 
what you do is. at a later point in ti me, if you have sold it for 100. six 
days later, that stock is 40, you can buy it for 40, and make sixty 
rupees overnight. Who makes those sixty rupees? Not the ordinary 
investor, because the ordinary investor does not know how the 
market is being manipulated. It is the broker who makes the sixty 
rupees. When you come to the other side of the picture, it is the bull 
who makes the money. Why? Because he buys long-term. Here, the 
bear sells short-term and the bull buys long-term. When the bull buys 
long-term, -the market rises. He buys at 50. But the problem is, the 
bull can't buy till he has the money, and no individual can have 300, 
400, 500, 600 crores to manipulat e the market. So, where does the 
bull get the money from? 
The bear gets the stock from the Stock-holding Corporation of 
India, but the bull has to have the money to buy. Where did he get the 
money from? That is where the othe r players come in, whether it is 
Global Trust or it is a financial institution or it is a bank lending. These 
big piayers give the money to the bull to buy long-term. They also 
make money in the process because they also have stock in their 
hands. So, what they do is, they lend it to the bull; the bull buys long-
term, buys at 50, and when the market goes to 100, sells it, dumps it 
at 100; makes that fifty rupees. T he crisis arose there because the 
bull who was buying, had reached the saturation point. The bull who 
was buying was raided by the inco me-tax authorities; the bull who 
was buying was said to owe Rs. 280 • 300 crores to the Income-tax 
Qepartment. The bull who was buying had to cut a cheque for Rs.26 
crores to buy peace. Then, what  happened? The market realised that 
the bull had no more money. So, let us dump his stocks. Global Trust 
realised that 'look we can't go with the bull anymore. We have lent 
him a lot of money; we can't go with the bull anymore.' So, they 
started demanding collateral from the bull. What was the result? 
When these stocks started going down, the stocks' selling started. 
That is how the whole scenario has come about where we see the 
ordinary middle class, the lower mi ddle class person who has put his 
savings, his life savings, in the stocks, not knowing when to sell and 
when to buy. And the loss of national  wealth is not the loss of the 
brokers,   as much as  it is the

SHRI S. VIDUTHALAI VIRUMBI (Tamil Nadu); Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, since morning, hon.  Members from both sides have 
been expressing their concern over th e volatility of the stock market 
which is unprecedented in India. Sir, both sides have said that they

stock market. Like the Kargil stand-o ff, this is also one of the national 
issues. Whenever national issues are debated in this august House, 
we find that there is unanimity in the thinking and this is what is called 
democracy, which we are having in our count cy. Sir, I do not want to 
go through or repeat what the other hon. Members have already 
expressed. The stock exchange episode came to light on 2 n March, 
2001, when the Sensex declined by 176 points. Then only the SEBI 
woke up and tried to find out the reasons for that. After 5 m of March, 
they decided to take some action. Sir, I do not want to go into the 
intricacies of what happened in the transactions, but, at the same 
time, I want to say that this type of manipulation should not take place 
hereafter, for which the Government of India, i.e., the Treasury 
Bencnes should take necessary steps. 
After its meeting of 5,n March, 2001, the SEBI has taken some 
action, whereby the counter-party guarantee has been introduced and 
the banks are allowed to provide collateral funding in the Automated 
Lending Borrowing Mechanism (ALBM) as well as in the Borrowing 
and Lending of Securities System  (BLESS); additional margin has 
been stipulated; outstanding limit has also  been curtailed, etc. Sir, all 
these steps have been taken subsequently, after this manipulation 
came to light. I would like to quote the second paragraph of the 
Statement which was made by the Fi nance Minister in the morning. I 
quote, "While the downward movem ent of the Indian stock market 
and its volatility have not been unusual compared to international 
markets, around the begi nning of March, 2001, ...," Had it been so, 
these type of measures ought not to  have been taken. Sir, when we 
have taken these measures, we foun d that there are some people 
who have indulged in some foul play . Sir, I feel that the message 
which should go today from this august House should be to 
strengthen the stock market, and set a healthy tradition in the stock 
market. And, tomorrow, I feel, it will take an upward turn and the 
status quo ante will be restored. Keeping that view in mind, I want to 
make some submissions. Sir, I would like to quote what Ms. Dina 
Mehta, the then President of the BSE said yesterday, and which 
appeared in today's newspapers.   I quote,

When the prices came down, the banks were alarmed. Some 
panic button was pressed. The bank s wanted to get the collateral 
security increased. For that purpo se, they pressed the people whom 
they had lent money to see that their securities were increased

nad stocks with them, whether they were willing or not, were

At the same time, in any system and in any area, this type of 
upheaval takes place. For example, in 1992, the former Prime 
Minister of the UK, Mr. Major, when he was the Lord Chancellor of the 
Exchequer, had actually put Britain into the bracket of the EERM. He 
had integrated the British system with the European exchange market 
mechanism. He thought that actually the sterling was pegged with the 
mark and the DM and that no devaluation would take place. When a 
journalist from The Sunday Times asked Major, when he was the

When this call was actually taken from Bonn, within hours, it had its 
own effect on Britain. Between 10.30 and 19.30 hours, the same day,

their own experience. Still, even Great  Britain was not able to control 
it. They lost nearly 4 billion sterling.  Therefore, this happens in every 
area and In every field. But we must take a lesson from this and see
